hook.reason: The title line "Three sodium out, two potassium in" is concrete, singable after one hearing, and opens and closes the chorus. But it names only the pump's count, one part of the cycle, and not the big move of spending energy to pile ions up so they rush back. The lesson opens on a real question ("Why does a neuron spend energy even when it's resting?"), and the narration opens on touching something hot, which comes from the learner's world.

frame.reason: The water tower is an apt whole-job picture (a pump spends energy uphill so that any open faucet rushes out), and it is set up early in the lesson, narration (n3-n4) and song (v1-1). It carries through the chorus ("Fill up the tower so the taps can run"), the outro, and the bridge ("the tower's down to a drip"). It maps cleanly onto the leaking and the stored energy. The mid-song verses on the cycle and the ouabain bridge lean on it less.

why_chain.reason: The lesson and narration walk through leak, then energy cost, then phosphorylation and shape change, then stored energy rushing when channels open, then resting potential and action potential, each with a "so". The song carries the gist. Link 5 is thinner: the lesson says K⁺ leaking out sets the resting potential but not why. It also does not say that the channels' selective permeability is what ties the gradient to the voltage. Link 4's statement that potassium leaks out is also only briefly explained.

key_lines.reason: They run in order and most are steps with arrows, such as "Ions leak back down gradients → pump must run nonstop" and "Sodium channels open → Na⁺ rushes in → action potential". Weaknesses: the first line is a question, not a step, and does not match the lyric it starts on. The second, "Water pump filling a tower = sodium-potassium pump", is a label. "ATP → ADP + Pᵢ" uses notation not in the lesson. The chain never reaches the stored-energy link, "gradients are stored energy → rush when channels open", and ends on the poison, not the core idea.

accuracy.reason: The facts are mostly right: the 3 Na⁺ out for 2 K⁺ in, one ATP per cycle, the 10× and 30× gradients, the resting potential set mainly by K⁺ leak, and the misconception about repolarization. The two items above are imprecisions, not real errors. The song's v1-7 "Foxglove gave a heart drug that slows this pump down" is fine. Saying that "Ouabain... locks the pump from outside" is also right.

singability.reason: The chorus is a strong, repeatable chant, and most lines are whole phrases that rhyme cleanly, such as "so the neuron's ready" and "the sodium floods in / the signal begins". Weaker points: the rhymes "inside / inside" (b-1/b-2) and "face / shape" (v1-5/v1-6) are slant or repeated; pre-chorus lines such as "The sodium gradient hauls glucose inside" read like facts; and several verse lines run long for the bar, such as v2-3 "It drops them in the cytoplasm, where potassium's packed". The verses also read as textbook captions in spots.

lesson_clarity.reason: It opens on a question, gives the big idea, builds on why with "so" links, and has a Predict question answered at once ("slightly more negative"). It names the misconception and why it is wrong, and ends on a good check ("why does stopping it eventually stop a neuron from firing?") that needs the core idea. Weaknesses: it adds many new terms (phosphorylation, resting membrane potential, secondary active transport, ATP synthase, osmosis) for high school, and side material such as glucose transport, mitochondria, and ouabain could be cut. The table also adds a list-like feel.

errors.claim: Lyric p1-2 "Potassium channels let it out and set it right" with p1-1 "It's not the pump that resets each spike" (pre-chorus)
errors.problem: The line is vague about what is let out and reset, and it can read as potassium channels restoring the gradients, when they only repolarize the membrane.
errors.correction: Say that potassium flowing out through its channels repolarizes the membrane, while the pump only restores the gradients slowly over many signals.

errors.claim: Lyric v2-4 "Three charges went out, only two came back" and narration n18 "Each cycle leaves the inside slightly more negative" (also the lesson's Predict)
errors.problem: This is correct, but a learner could carry away that the pump itself mainly makes the resting potential. It is hedged in the lesson, not in the song.
errors.correction: In the song, add that the pump's own contribution is only a few millivolts.

topics.core_idea: The pump spends ATP to keep sodium piled outside and potassium inside, so ions rush back whenever channels open.
why_chain: Ions slowly leak back through ion channels, so without a pump the sodium and potassium gradients would run down.
Pushing ions against their concentration gradients takes energy, so the pump does active transport and spends one ATP per cycle.
ATP's phosphate attaches to the pump and changes its shape, so it carries three sodium out and then two potassium in.
The piled-up ions are stored energy, so when ion channels open, sodium rushes in and potassium leaks out.
Potassium leaking out sets the resting membrane potential, and sodium rushing in fires an action potential.
topics.title_line: Three sodium out, two potassium in

topics.subject: biology

problems: v1-2 lyric-style: "So you swap it at the booth for two kinds of cash today" runs 13 words, over 12

hook.reason: The title line "Split the water, catch the light" is two concrete actions on real things, short, easy to sing back, and it names the big move. It opens and closes the chorus. The lesson opens on a real question, "Where does the oxygen in your next breath come from?", and the narration opens on "The oxygen in every breath you take", which is from the learner's world. The line names the water-splitting and light-capture end of the idea but not the electron flow or the cash-in, so it is not the full core idea in miniature.

frame.reason: The currency exchange booth fits the whole job ("trade the energy of light for two currencies the cell can spend"), with the Calvin cycle as the market stall that spends the cash. It is set up in the song's intro ("Sunshine's money that a leaf can't spend outright") and carried through the chorus ("that's the deal"), the bridge ("the trade breaks down") and the outro. The lesson and narration use it too. It is a little thinner in the middle steps, where the electrons and the pump get stairs rather than money, but the stairs are a part-picture that fits inside the frame.

why_chain.reason: The lesson and narration teach every link in order with causes: electrons leave, "so" water is split to replace them, the energy released pumps H⁺, photosystem I re-energizes them for NADPH, piled-up H⁺ can only leave through ATP synthase, which spins, and the Calvin cycle spends both currencies. The herbicide case then traces the chain backwards, which tests it. The song carries the gist. The one soft spot is the claim that photosystem I needs light to excite electrons "giving them the energy needed to make NADPH", which is stated rather than explained. It is still a clear cause.

key_lines.reason: They run from the question through the steps to the herbicide case, and most are steps with arrows. But the first, "How does a leaf turn light into usable energy?", is a question, not a step, and the second, "Exchange booth = thylakoid, market stall = Calvin cycle", is a label. The Calvin line starts at p2-1 and has no narration anchor, and the proton-gradient line starts at v2-5 where the song never says what the protons do next. The "H⁺ flows through ATP synthase → ATP" step is therefore not said where it appears, and the final line is a herbicide application, not the core idea.

accuracy.reason: The science is sound at AP level: water as the source of O₂, b6f as the only pump, ATP synthase spinning, chemiosmosis, the herbicide chain, and the numbering explanation are all correct. The song's chorus shorthand "Electrons fall and pack the protons tight" and "Protons spin ATP synthase like a wheel" compress the mechanism and could be tightened, but nothing a learner would carry away wrong. The lyric "Found second, so they named it two, though it's first in time" garbles the discovery-order fact, since photosystem I was discovered first, so "found second" is misleading. That is one real imprecision.

singability.reason: The chorus is a strong chant ("Split the water, catch the light / ... that's the deal") with clean rhymes and short lines. The verses are rapped and mostly fit, with some run-ons like "Both currencies drop out into the stroma, ready to spend" and "Where the sugar-building starts and the light part ends" that read as caption lines. Several lines rhyme weakly or bend for rhyme ("two" / "first in time", "ADP" / "currency"). The pre-chorus lines such as "The oxygen you breathe was water, not CO2" are textbook-sounding. The bridge lines are a flat list of consequences, and b-2 "the electrons can't get out" does not rhyme with b-1.

lesson_clarity.reason: It opens on a question, gives the big picture with the exchange booth, builds on why each step happens, and has a labeled **Predict:** question answered right away ("H⁺ keeps piling up in the lumen. What will it do?"). It names the misconception and says where the oxygen comes from, and ends on a check that needs the core idea ("Why would ATP synthase soon stop making ATP if a plant were kept in the dark"). Its weaker side is the number of new terms for a first-time learner (photosystems, b6f, NADP⁺ reductase, chemiosmosis, lumen, stroma) and the aside on numbering and the mitochondria section, which could be cut. The misconception is stated but the reason it is wrong is only "it comes from water", not why.

errors.claim: Lyric v1-12: "And each step down powers the pump to push more protons there" and v1-9 "Oxygen floats off, and protons pile in the lumen" followed by c1-2 "Electrons fall and pack the protons tight"
errors.problem: The chorus says the falling electrons directly pack the protons, skipping that water splitting also adds H⁺ and that b6f is what pumps them. This is a shorthand that could be taken as electrons physically packing protons.
errors.correction: Electrons falling powers cytochrome b6f, which pumps H⁺ into the lumen.

errors.claim: Lyric v2-3 "On the stroma side, they're loaded onto NADP plus" and key line "Light re-energizes electrons at photosystem I → NADPH"
errors.problem: This is a minor gap: the electrons reach NADP⁺ by way of ferredoxin and NADP⁺ reductase, and it is not stated that H⁺ is also needed. It is a fair simplification for the level, so it is only a small imprecision.
errors.correction: Say that NADP⁺ reductase uses two electrons and an H⁺ to make NADPH (as the narration does).

topics.core_idea: Light pulls electrons from water, and their flow downhill is cashed in for ATP and NADPH.
why_chain: Light excites electrons in photosystem II, so they leave, and it splits water to replace them, releasing O₂ and H⁺.
The electrons fall to lower energy down the electron transport chain, and that energy lets cytochrome b6f pump H⁺ into the lumen.
Light re-energizes the electrons at photosystem I, giving them the energy to turn NADP⁺ into NADPH.
H⁺ piled up in the lumen can only flow back out through ATP synthase, so its flow spins it and makes ATP.
ATP and NADPH go into the stroma, where the Calvin cycle spends them to build sugar.
topics.title_line: Split the water, catch the light

topics.subject: calculus

problems: v2-5 lyric-style: "Zoom way in on a smooth curve, it starts to look straight," narrates the picture instead of being sung
v2-7 lyric-style: "Do it at every x, and you get a new function, f prime," runs 13 words, over 12
b-4 motion: 5 lines in a row from b-4 with nothing moving, on a scene where things travel

hook.reason: The title line "Shrink the gap and read the speed" is concrete, short, singable, and holds the core idea in miniature, opening and closing the chorus. The lesson opens on a real question, "How can a car have a speed at one single instant...", and the narration opens on "Picture a car on the highway: how fast is it going right now?" Both are strong. "Read the speed" leans a bit on the dashboard, and "the gap" is abstract before the picture is set, so it falls just short of the model.

frame.reason: The odometer/speedometer dashboard is an apt picture of the whole idea: a rate of a running total at this instant. It is set up in the lesson, the narration (n2-n4) and song verse 1, and it recurs in the pre-chorus ("Parked with miles, the speedometer still reads zero") and in the title line. The chorus, bridge and outro drift to secant, tangent and slopes, so the car is not carried through the whole song. The verse 2 and bridge material is mostly graph language.

why_chain.reason: All five links are taught in order with causes in both lesson and narration: "One point alone has no change to divide", "An average hides the details", "the second point slides... so the secant line tips toward the tangent line", "You can't just set h = 0... 0/0", "That limit is the derivative". The song carries the gist in verse 1, verse 2 and the chorus. The reason the limit is needed (0/0) is stated, and the worked table shows the slopes settling. One small gap: it never says why the settling number must be the tangent slope beyond the zoom-in remark.

key_lines.reason: Read in order, they tell the chain well: "An average over a long gap hides the changes", "Shrink the gap → secant line tips toward tangent line", "h = 0 gives 0/0, so derivative = limit of slopes". But the first, "How do you find a rate at one instant?", is a question rather than a step. Several are misaligned. "Tangent line slope = instantaneous rate of change" starts at the zoom-in line v2-5. "Shrink the gap → secant line tips..." starts at narration n11, a question that does not state it. The last two (f′(x)/power rule and the corner) add material beyond the core chain, and "Corner: slopes 1 and −1 disagree" is long.

accuracy.reason: Facts check out: difference quotient 6 + h, slopes 7/6.1/6.01, f′(x) = 2x, |x| slopes ±1, the 0/0 point, and the sign meaning. The lesson honestly flags the smooth-graph simplification. Song line v2-6 says "that line's slope is the rate" and p1-1 "how fast, not how far" are fine. Nothing a learner would carry away wrong.

singability.reason: Much of the chorus is a chant, with "Shrink the gap and read the speed" repeated as a hook. But many lines overrun the bar badly: "Its slope's the average rate of change, rise over run too", "Do it at every x, and you get a new function, f prime", and the bridge lines "No limit means no derivative where the corner sits". Some read like textbook captions: "Absolute value of x has a sharp corner at zero". Some rhymes are forced or bend meaning: "rise over run too" (filler to rhyme with "through"), "slopes approach" with "zero's no hope", and "slopes can rest" with "flips". c2 "settle down / right now" are fine, but c3-1 and c3-2 add a long extra chorus.

lesson_clarity.reason: It opens on a question, gives the picture, builds step by step on why, asks "What do you think happens to the secant line as the points close in?" and answers it immediately, and names the misconception with the parked-car reason. It ends on a check that needs understanding: why |x| has no derivative at 0 when it has one at 2. Weaknesses: a long run of terms (difference quotient, secant, tangent, limit, instantaneous rate, f′), and extras such as the power rule, sign, local linearity and the corner section that a first-time learner may not need. The misconception comes late, after those extras.

topics.core_idea: Shrink the gap between two points, and their average slope settles on the derivative: the rate of change right now.
why_chain: One point alone has no change to divide, so a rate needs two points: the average rate of change, the secant line's slope.
An average over a long gap hides the speeding up and slowing down inside it, so we want a smaller gap.
Shrinking the gap slides the second point toward the first, so the secant line tips toward the tangent line.
Setting the gap to zero gives 0/0, so the derivative is the limit: the number the average slopes settle on.
That limit is the tangent line's slope, the instantaneous rate of change, just as a speedometer reads the odometer's rate right now.
topics.title_line: Shrink the gap and read the speed,

topics.subject: history

hook.reason: The title line "The crown went broke, the people rose" is concrete and singable, and it opens and closes the chorus. But it names only the start and the end, "the crown went broke" and "the people rose", and it skips the Estates-General turn, so it isn't the core idea in miniature. The lesson opens on a real question ("How does a government run out of money and end up handing power to an assembly?"). The narration opens on bread eating half a family's income, which is from the learner's world, though that is a strong image the song's intro barely uses.

frame.reason: The dinner table with an unpaid bill is an apt picture of the whole thing: who pays, who votes, and who walks away to start their own table. The lesson, the narration (n4-n6) and the first verse all use it. But it is dropped after verse 1: the chorus, bridge and outro don't mention diners or a table, and the lesson never uses it again after its own section. The bread, Bastille and England parts sit outside the picture.

why_chain.reason: The lesson and narration give the causes in order: wars lead to debt, the privileged refuse to pay, so the king calls the Estates-General, voting by order lets the privileged outvote the Third, so it declares the National Assembly. n13 asks "why didn't the king just tax..." and answers it. The last link is thinner. The bread link says crowds "backed the Assembly" and stormed the Bastille, but it doesn't clearly connect hunger and troop movements to backing the Assembly. The Enlightenment is a bare statement rather than a link. Core idea "seize power" is only implied by the assembly declaration. The England section adds an analogy, but it doesn't complete the chain.

key_lines.reason: Most are steps in order: "Privileged refuse new taxes → king calls Estates-General", "Vote by order: First and Second outvote Third Estate". Several start where the step is sung or said. But the first, "Why did the French Revolution break out in 1789?", is a question rather than a step. "Unpaid bill = the crown's war debt" is a label. The last two ("Next: privileges abolished..." and "England 1640...") are off the core chain. The chain's final links, the Third Estate seizing power and the Bastille, are squeezed into one line.

accuracy.reason: Dates, the 1614 meeting, voting by order, the tennis court and the Bastille's seven prisoners are all correct, and the misconception is handled well. The one issue is that "Enlightenment says the power comes from the people" gives only one thinker's view as the whole movement. The song's "Third Estate breaks off, speaks the nation's will" is fair. Also, "Two beat one, so the Third can't win a thing" is loose but fair for the level. A teacher might tighten the Enlightenment line, but nothing wrong is carried away.

singability.reason: The chorus is a chant a learner could sing back after two hearings, and the rhymes are mostly clean. But many verse lines read like captions or run long: "Enlightenment says the power comes from the people, so" and "Third Estate's ninety-seven percent, and they carry the load". The rhyme at v2-3/v2-4, "so" and "whole", is forced. Rhymes like "fight" and "tight" and "dies" and "side" bend the sentence: "the crown can't hold the city tight" is awkward. The bridge is a narrated recap of the English story, which is a list of events. The first verses carry the term list ("First Estate's the clergy") as definitions.

lesson_clarity.reason: It opens on a question, gives the big picture and the dinner picture, and handles the misconception ("France was one of Europe's richest kingdoms") clearly. It asks one prediction question ("What do you think its deputies did next?") and answers it right after. The closing check, "If the First and Second Estates had agreed to pay new taxes in 1787, why might the Estates-General never have been called?", can be answered only by a learner who understands the chain. But the lesson carries many terms and dates, plus the England section and the "What comes next" section, which pad it. The table is a list of parts, but it supports the why. It is mostly clear, with some things worth cutting.

errors.claim: Lesson and n1/i-2/o-1: "bread could eat up more than half of a working family's income" used as the song's opening while the intro also says "Bread cost over half your pay"
errors.problem: Mildly misleading ordering: it presents the bread crisis as the first reason in the intro, while the lesson's own chain and the core idea put the debt first. This is a framing issue rather than a factual error, so no correction is needed beyond the wording.

errors.claim: Song v2-3 to v2-4: "Enlightenment says the power comes from the people" (applied as all of the Enlightenment)
errors.problem: The lesson and song credit only Rousseau's idea, which gives the Enlightenment as a single claim; Montesquieu and rights were also part of it, a simplification.
errors.correction: Say Enlightenment thinkers argued that power comes from the people and should be limited.

topics.core_idea: The crown went broke, the privileged refused to pay, so calling the Estates-General let the Third Estate seize power.
why_chain: Costly wars, including aid to the American Revolution, left the French crown deep in debt.
The crown could not raise taxes because the First and Second Estates paid little and refused new ones.
Out of options, the king called the Estates-General in 1789, the first since 1614.
Voting by order let the privileged outvote the Third Estate, which, armed with Enlightenment ideas, declared itself the National Assembly.
Soaring bread prices angered Paris, so crowds backed the Assembly and stormed the Bastille.
topics.title_line: The crown went broke, the people rose

topics.subject: literature
topics.topic: dramatic irony in Romeo and Juliet

hook.reason: The title line "We see the trap, Romeo walks in" is concrete, singable and bookends the chorus, but it names the trap rather than the big move, and "trap" is left vague at the start. The lesson opens on a real question ("Why would Shakespeare give away his ending before the play even starts?") and the narration opens in the learner's world ("Picture a scary movie"), which are both strong.

frame.reason: The scary-movie picture ("a shadow in the hall", "yell at the screen") fits the whole idea, because the audience sees danger the character can't and cannot warn them. It is set up in the intro, the verse, the lesson, the narration and the outro, and it returns in c3-2. It is somewhat familiar as a way to explain irony, but it does the job of the whole thing, not one part. The bridge and the irony-types section drift away from it.

why_chain.reason: The chain runs Prologue, then secrets, then darker meanings, then no warning, then suspense and dread, then the tomb, and the lesson and narration teach it in order. The causes are stated ("Because we know more... we can't warn them, so suspense and dread build"). Link 3 is only asserted: no worked example shows a hopeful line turning dark, so how words gain a second meaning is named rather than shown. The long plot recap (Tybalt, Mercutio, quarantine) carries the story more than the causes, which dilutes the chain.

key_lines.reason: The lines are mostly steps with arrows ("Prologue gives away the ending → we know they'll die", "Letter stuck in quarantine → Romeo hears only that she died") and they read in order toward the peak. Several problems remain. The first is a question, not a step. "Not a surprise twist" is a misconception line placed mid-chain. The v2-1 line "We know more → their hopeful plans fill us with dread" starts on a lyric about Paris that does not say it. The Oedipus line adds a term-free but off-chain step, and the chain never states the core idea in a final line.

accuracy.reason: The plot and the idea are sound: dramatic irony is correctly defined, the Prologue, the secret marriage, the quarantined Friar John, the potion and the Oedipus myth are all accurate. The errors I listed are minor or contested, not facts the learner would carry away wrong. Two small imprecisions remain: "we know the ending before it begins" and the chorus's "every sweet word" are broader than strictly needed, and "Romeo walks in" sidelines Juliet, who also acts in ignorance. The sonnet's own line says the lovers' deaths end the feud, which the droplet only half uses.

singability.reason: The chorus is a clean, repeatable chant ("We see the trap, Romeo walks in / We know the ending before it begins"), and most verse lines sit in a rapped bar. Several lines are plot summary overrunning the bar or reading like captions, such as v2-4 "But the letter from Verona's stuck in quarantine instead" (a rhyme-driven "instead") and v2-7 "We know she's only sleeping as he drinks the poison dry". The pre-chorus pc2-1/2 is textbook ("It's one of three kinds, there's verbal irony too"), and c3-1/c3-2 add lines that crowd the chorus.

lesson_clarity.reason: It opens on a question, gives the big idea, uses the scary-movie picture, includes a Predict question answered right after, and names the misconception with its reason. It ends on a check that needs the core idea: "If the audience didn't know about Juliet's potion, would Romeo's death... still be dramatic irony?" The plot recap and the table are long, the Oedipus and three-types sections add terms (verbal, situational) a first-time learner doesn't need, and the Predict question is about Tybalt, which is a plot fact, not the core idea.

errors.claim: Song intro i-2 and chorus: "You yell at the screen, but they can't hear a thing" / "We see the trap, Romeo walks in" combined with narration n20 "a servant brings news to Mantua that she is dead" and lesson "the tomb... Juliet is only asleep from a potion" as who doesn't know
errors.problem: The lesson table and chain say the tomb irony is that Romeo doesn't know, but the lesson omits that Romeo never received the Friar's letter was the gap that matters, and the song's v2-7 "as he drinks the poison dry" is fine; the real misleading item is the lesson's statement that Tybalt and Mercutio 'do not know why' alongside the claim Romeo kills Tybalt after Mercutio dies without noting Romeo's refusal was to Tybalt's challenge being a response to Romeo's earlier insult.
errors.correction: No change needed to the tomb; if kept, note that Romeo's refusal is the irony and that Mercutio only dies because he steps in.

errors.claim: Song c3-1 "From the first lines to the tomb, we knew more"
errors.problem: Minor: Romeo isn't the only one walking in; the 'trap' is not named, but more importantly 'Romeo walks in' omits Juliet, who is equally unaware of the fate.
errors.correction: Say "they walk in" or name both lovers.

topics.core_idea: Dramatic irony: we know what the characters don't, so we watch them walk into danger and feel the dread.
why_chain: The Prologue tells the audience at the start that the star-crossed lovers will die.
Then the audience sees secrets the characters miss, like the secret marriage and the sleeping potion.
Because the audience knows more, the characters' hopeful words and plans take on a darker meaning.
The audience can't warn them, so suspense and dread build with every step toward the tomb.
In the tomb the gap is widest: Romeo thinks Juliet is dead, but the audience knows she is asleep.
topics.title_line: We see the trap, Romeo walks in

topics.subject: chemistry
topics.topic: how a catalyst speeds up a reaction

hook.reason: The title line "Take the low pass, let molecules cross" is concrete, singable and names the big move, though it is nearly the core idea in miniature rather than fully so (it leaves out the barrier and the collisions). The lesson opens on a real question ("Why does hydrogen peroxide sit almost unchanged in its bottle, yet fizz into foam the moment it touches a cut?") and the narration opens on peroxide on a cut, which is from the learner's world. The one weakness is that "low pass" needs the hiking picture to land.

frame.reason: The hike from one valley over a mountain to a lower valley, with a lower pass trail, is apt for the whole idea and not a stock picture. The song sets it up in v1-1 to v1-4 and carries it through the chorus, bridge ("the low pass is closed") and outro. The lesson and narration (n5-n8) use it too. It loosens in the middle verses and in the converter section, where the pass trail is not tied to the surface mechanism, and the chorus's "catalyst comes back around" sits outside the picture.

why_chain.reason: The lesson and narration teach all five links in order, each with its cause: collisions need Ea, few have it so the reaction is slow, the new mechanism lowers Ea, a larger fraction succeed so k rises, and the energies stay put so equilibrium does not shift. The two-step iodide example shows how the catalyst is regenerated. The narration even asks "So what happens to the rate when the barrier is lower?". The song carries the gist. The order is slightly scrambled in the narration, where the equilibrium link (n19-n21) comes before the rate result (n23).

key_lines.reason: Read in order they cover the chain well: "High barrier → few collisions have enough energy → slow", "Lower activation energy → more successful collisions → larger rate constant". But the first, "How does a catalyst make a reaction faster?", is a question, not a step. "Summit trail = no catalyst; Pass trail = catalyst's lower path" is a label. "Same ΔH, both directions sped → equilibrium unchanged" starts at p1-1 "cuts the climb both ways the same" and so overstates what is sung. "I⁻ used in Step 1, given back in Step 2" starts at v1-7 and n15, which only covers step 1. Several lines also carry terms like "Platinum surface: CO + O₂ → CO₂" and are not in chain order (the rate-constant line comes after the equilibrium line).

accuracy.reason: The content is sound: activation energy, transition state, Arrhenius, the iodide mechanism with intermediate and catalyst identified correctly, ΔH and K unchanged, and lead poisoning of the converter. There is one small imprecision in the song (v2-4/v2-5), which says oxygen "joins in" without saying it also adsorbs, and the chorus wording "same reactants in, same products out" is a loose way to say the energies stay the same. Nothing a learner would carry away wrong.

singability.reason: The chorus is a strong chant ("Take the low pass, let molecules cross") and most lines fit the bar. Several rapped lines read like captions or run long ("Carbon monoxide lands on the metal and it sticks", "Keep the platinum clean, and the low pass lets them pass"). The rhymes are sometimes weak or bent: "in the way / stay" is fine, but "ready for some more / less CO than before" and "cleanup's lost" with "cross" reach for the rhyme. The chorus has five lines plus a different extended third chorus, which makes it harder to sing back. "CO2" and "Step 1" are written as notation rather than as a singer says them.

lesson_clarity.reason: It opens on a question, gives the big idea and the hiking picture, and builds on the why in numbered steps. "Same drool: food → UR, tone → CR" has no narration anchor, and the end of the chain, "suppressed, not erased", is not tied to the core idea. They also carry many terms.

accuracy.reason: The facts, terms and examples match the study guide. The one imprecision is the chorus c3-1 "Neutral tone plus food", which loses the "just before" timing the guide stresses. Nothing else would leave a learner with a wrong idea. The song's "Operant's the other kind: what you do, and what it brings" is fair for the level.

singability.reason: The chorus is a chant that is easy to sing back, and "Ring the bell, then bring the meal" is clean. The rapped verses mostly stay close to the bar. Several lines read like textbook captions: "Food's the unconditioned stimulus, nobody had to teach it" and "Drool's the unconditioned response, automatic when they eat it" are long, and "it eat it" rhymes bend the grammar. Terms like "U-R" and "C-R" are spelled as sung. c3-1 and c3-2 are a clunky addition to the chorus and are not a clean chant. The pre-chorus "Here two stimuli get paired, the drool's an automatic thing" is stiff.

lesson_clarity.reason: It opens on the question "Why does a bell make you hungry?", gives the big idea, then builds the why step by step. It asks a prediction question ("What do you think the dog does now when it hears the tone by itself?"), answers it directly, names the misconception and says why it is wrong, and closes with a check that requires the "no longer predicts" idea. It carries a lot of terms (US, UR, NS, CS, CR, acquisition, extinction, spontaneous recovery, operant) plus Little Albert and Garcia, which is heavy for a first read, and the "You've felt this" section is somewhat of a list.

errors.claim: Song v1-3 to v1-4: "Pavlov studied digestion when his dogs went off script / They drooled at the feeder's footsteps before the food hit their lips"
errors.problem: Mostly fine, but the chorus c3-1 "Neutral tone plus food, now the tone works alone" compresses the sequence and drops the order (tone before food) that matters.
errors.correction: Say "Neutral tone, then food" so the order is kept.

topics.core_idea: A signal that keeps coming right before something meaningful starts to predict it, so it triggers the response alone.
why_chain: Food triggers drooling automatically, because it is an unconditioned stimulus that needs no learning.
A tone triggers nothing at first, because as a neutral stimulus it does not yet signal anything.
When the tone keeps coming just before the food, the dog learns that the tone predicts the food.
So the tone becomes a conditioned stimulus that triggers drooling on its own, a conditioned response.
If the tone keeps sounding without food, the drooling fades, because the tone no longer predicts the food.
topics.title_line: Ring the bell, then bring the meal
